extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals (PRSA members and other PR practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Field-level ethical guidance from PRSA's Board of Ethics and Professional Standards (BEPS) covering pay-for-play, social media, plagiarism, influencers, native advertising, AI accountability, leaks and related conduct for PR practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose, scope and limits of the PRSA Code of Ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: The PRSA Code of Ethics exists to inspire ethical behavior, clearly identify improper public relations practices and teach members how to avoid them. As a voluntary organization PRSA can establish voluntary practice standards, codes of conduct and practice guidelines, inspire and educate best practice, promote voluntary compliance and establish ethical practice as the most important obligation of a PRSA member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRSA's enforcement authority is limited — it cannot impose government-level sanctions; organizations with regulatory enforcement gain power from legislation or executive authority. The Code establishes what is unethical (threats to ethical practice, behaviors inconsistent with the Code, disruptive behaviors, practices destructive to reputations) and provides education and limited procedures for membership actions. Use the Code as an aspirational and practical guide; consult BEPS for advisories and clarifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay-for-Play
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay-for-play is when payment (monetary or other compensation) is made to a media channel or content provider in return for coverage or visibility without transparent disclosure, causing consumers to believe content was selected on its merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BEPS's position: pay-for-play conflicts with PRSA Code provisions (Free Flow of Information; Disclosure of Information; Conflicts of Interest; Enhancing the Profession) and PRSA values (Honesty, Fairness, Independence). To avoid: request and include disclosure whenever compensation is provided for exposure; encourage disclosure of travel, lodging, gifts, non-monetary compensation by recipients; always promote clear and obvious disclosure of material value provided in exchange for coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and Social Media (use of social platforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners must apply the PRSA Code of Ethics to social media — adopting a higher standard than that of the general public and recognizing the increased speed, reach and risks of social platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant Code provisions: Disclosure of Information; Safeguarding Confidences; Conflicts of Interest; Enhancing the Profession. Practitioners should: fully disclose paid placements and associations with products; protect confidential, private and proprietary information (recognize risk of improper disclosure); be aware of employee free-speech protections (NLRB); disclose conflicts when communicating or working with influencers; ensure gifts are nominal, legal and infrequent; use social media to inform and educate about the profession. BEPS recommends treating trust as the ultimate currency on social media and applying transparency and the Code in all digital activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism is the unauthorized use or close imitation of another's language or ideas and representing them as one's own; both inadvertent and intentional plagiarism are ethically unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BEPS states inadvertent plagiarism carries equal ethical weight with intentional misrepresentation. Related Code provisions: Free Flow of Information; Competition; Disclosure of Information; Conflicts of Interest. Professional values implicated: Honesty, Expertise, Fairness. To avoid plagiarism: do not copy sentences, paragraphs or documents from other sources; paraphrase in your own words and credit the original creator; use quotation marks and citations for exact wording; when using internet sources assume someone created the content and give proper credit and attribution; disclose all sources and obtain permission/licensing when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid Spokespersons and Influencers (disclosure of paid relationships)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone paid to serve as a spokesperson, advocate or influencer for an organization must disclose the contractual relationship or compensation arrangement to audiences so they can make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies Code provisions: Disclosure of Information; Conflicts of Interest; Enhancing the Profession. BEPS recommends: disclose commercial relationships in advance of or simultaneous to public appearances or content; ensure all parties in the contractual chain disclose the relationship; be honest and accurate about sponsors and financial interests; reveal any material interest that could influence commentary or endorsements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representing Front Groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Front groups are organizations structured or labeled to mislead the public about their true mission; assisting or creating them to hide intent is deceptive and a violation of ethical standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conduct conflicts with PRSA Code provisions (Free Flow of Information; Disclosure of Information; Conflicts of Interest; Enhancing the Profession) and values (Honesty, Fairness, Advocacy). BEPS recommends: avoid assisting front groups or participating in undisclosed sponsorships or deceptive descriptions of goals, tactics, sponsors or participants even if activities are lawful; prioritize open communication and transparency to support informed decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overstating Fees or Compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming compensation, credit, or delivering invoices for work not performed (inflating charges or overstating fees) is unethical and can be illegal; it harms the profession's trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary Code provision: Enhancing the Profession; values: Honesty, Fairness, Loyalty. BEPS position: members should charge clients only for services rendered and in accordance with contracts, correctly report time and expenses, and avoid inflating charges or supporting data. Remedy: maintain accurate billing records, adhere to contracts and organizational billing procedures, and commit to high standards of integrity in financial reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native Advertising & Sponsored Content (distinguish paid vs. organic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that is sponsored or paid-for but mimics organic editorial content must be clearly and conspicuously disclosed so consumers can distinguish paid content from independent editorial material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant Code provisions: Disclosure of Information; Free Flow of Information; Competition; Conflicts of Interest; Enhancing the Profession. BEPS recommends: ensure sponsorship is fully disclosed in the context of the content and appropriate to the medium; make sponsored content easily discernible from organic content; disclosures should effectively differentiate paid content and not attempt to deceive consumers about independence or editorial selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI and Leadership Accountabilities (machine learning accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: When AI or machine learning systems make decisions that affect people or organizations, ultimate accountability should rest with human leaders who have oversight responsibility at the time of the mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BEPS notes that machines cannot be held responsible in the same way humans can; Code provisions implicated include Disclosure of Information, Free Flow of Information, Conflicts of Interest, Enhancing the Profession; values include Honesty, Advocacy, Fairness. Recommendations: counsel senior leadership that human beings remain accountable for machine-made decisions; draw clear lines of human responsibility and oversight; present these lines transparently in communications and in response plans; identify root causes and corrective actions and communicate them openly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Media as a Reflection of Majority Opinion (caution in interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media activity is often driven by a small, highly active minority and therefore is not a reliable or scientific indicator of majority public opinion; practitioners should avoid presenting it as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BEPS's position: when sharing analysis based on social media, remind audiences that the platform is informal, nonscientific evidence and may not reflect majority sentiment. Related Code provisions: Free Flow of Information; Disclosure of Information; Enhancing the Profession. Practitioners should contextualize social-media-derived conclusions and avoid overstating representativeness or extrapolating viral activity to the general public without proper caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Leaks (protect confidentiality and follow approval processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: PR professionals should refrain from leaking confidential or proprietary information to media or other stakeholders without expressed approval from organizational leadership — leaks undermine trust and can be illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant Code provisions: Safeguarding Confidence; Disclosure of Information; Free Flow of Information; Conflicts of Interest; Enhancing the Profession. BEPS recommends: be fully aware of laws, regulations, contracts and business terms governing information flow; adhere to contractual and legal obligations protecting confidentiality; never independently share information obtained in confidence; follow standing approval procedures for disclosures; understand potential civil/criminal penalties for unlawful leaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical Standards Advisories (ESAs) — BEPS guidance mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: BEPS issues Ethical Standards Advisories (ESAs) to provide guidance within the framework of the PRSA Code of Ethics as issues arise; ESAs are informational and not legal advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ESAs summarize BEPS positions on emerging ethical topics (e.g., misinformation ESA, pay-for-play, social media) and provide recommended practices. Some ESAs and resources are available to PRSA/PRSSA members via MyPRSA. For questions or concerns practitioners may contact BEPS (beps@prsa.org) and should allow time for response (BEPS is volunteer-run). ESAs are intended to assist members in applying the Code, not to substitute for legal counsel where laws apply.
